title: East Pacific Rise
sentences: The East Pacific Rise (EPR) is a mid-ocean rise at a divergent tectonic plate boundary, located along the floor of the Pacific Ocean.
It is usually termed an oceanic rise and not a mid-ocean ridge due to its higher rate of spreading, which results in less elevation increase and more regular terrain.
Spreading rates vary along the East Pacific Rise, ranging from superfast in the south (>130-150 mm/yr), to fast in the north (90-130 mm/yr).
The EPR separates the Pacific plate to the west from the North American plate, the Rivera plate, the Cocos plate, the Nazca plate, and the Antarctic plate (listed from north to south).

It runs south from the Gulf of California in the Salton Sea basin in Southern California to a point near 55°S 130°W, where it joins the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge (PAR) trending west-south-west towards Antarctica, near New Zealand (though in some uses the PAR is regarded as the southern section of the EPR).
Much of the rise lies about 3,200 km (2,000 mi) off the South American coast and reaches a height about 1,800–2,700 m (5,900–8,900 ft) above the surrounding seafloor.
The EPR is a region of active, effusive volcanism.
As a result of this subterranean heat, hydrothermal activity in the EPR provides the temperatures, nutrients, and protection that many species of thermophilic organisms need to survive.
The oceanic crust is moving away from the East Pacific Rise to either side.
Near Easter Island the rate is over 150 mm (6 in) per year which is the fastest in the world.
However, on the northern end, it is much slower at only roughly 60 mm (2+1⁄2 in) per year.
On the eastern side of the rise, the eastward-moving Cocos and Nazca plates meet the westward moving South American plate and the North American plate and are being subducted under them.
The belt of volcanos along the Andes and the arc of volcanoes through Central America and Mexico are the direct results of this collision.
Due east of the Baja California peninsula, the Rise is sometimes referred to as the Gulf of California Rift Zone.
In this area, newly formed oceanic crust is intermingled with rifted continental crust originating from the North American plate.

Near Easter Island, the East Pacific Rise meets the Chile Rise at the Easter Island and Juan Fernandez microplates, trending off to the east where it subducts under the South American plate at the Peru–Chile Trench along the coast of southern Chile.
This portion of the Rise has been referred to as the Cape Adare-Easter Island Ridge, Albatross Cordillera, Easter Island Cordillera, Easter Island Rise, and Easter Island Swell.
Parts of the East Pacific Rise have oblique spreading, such as the Nazca–Pacific plate boundary between 29°S and 32°S.
This is seafloor spreading that is not orthogonal to the nearest ridge segment.
The southern extension of the East Pacific Rise (the PAR) merges with the Southeast Indian Ridge at the Macquarie triple junction south of New Zealand.
The southern stretch of the East Pacific Rise is also one of the fastest-spreading divergent boundaries on Earth, peaking at 79.3 mm (3.12 in)/year.
Along the East Pacific Rise the hydrothermal vents called black smokers were first discovered by the RISE project in 1979, and have since been extensively studied.
These vents are forming volcanogenic massive sulfide ore deposits on the ocean floor.
Many unique deep-water creatures have been found with vents, that subsist in a chemosynthetic ecosystem rather than one using photosynthesis.
The history of the East Pacific Rise is closely related to the evolution of the ancient Farallon plate and the ensuing plate reorganizations of the eastern Pacific plate system.
Evidence of these reorganizations comes from the topography of the Pacific ocean and magnetic lineations across the seafloor.
There is evidence of several ancient spreading centers and fracture zones caused by these reorganizations, which allow us to constrain the locations of the ancient plates.
Around 30 million years ago, there was a collision between the Pacific–Farallon spreading ridge and the North American margin.
This caused a major reorganization of the northeastern Pacific plate system, and the Farallon plate began to fragment.

Around 25 million years ago, this reorganization and fragmentation resulted in the formation of the Guadalupe plate, an ancient microplate bounded by the Murray fracture zone to its north and the Cocos-Nazca spreading ridge to its south.

Around 23 million years ago, the ancient Farallon plate subducted under the North American plate faster than it could regenerate, which caused the Farallon plate to break into two smaller plates, or the Nazca and Cocos plates.
This was likely driven by the divergence of slab-pull stresses at the subduction zones in Middle America and South America.
Another reorganization occurred between 12.5 and 11 million years ago, which resulted in the reduction in size of the Nazca-Cocos plate boundary.
This ridge was originally located over the Mathematicians seamounts.
At this same time, the Pacific-Guadalupe spreading center likely died out between latitudes of 29°30′N to 23°30′N.
The Farallon plate continued to fragment between 6.5 and 3.5 million years ago, and the plates reorganized, leaving behind extinct seafloor spreading centers like the Mathematician Ridge.
A major reorganization occurred around 2.5 million years ago, where the Pacific-Cocos spreading center moved north towards the Rivera fracture zone.
Together, these events contributed to the development of a new crustal accretion center between the Pacific, Nazca, and Cocos plates, which became the modern East Pacific Rise.
The EPR remains an active divergent plate boundary to this day.

The East Pacific Rise is considered a fast to very-fast spreading mid-ocean ridge, meaning it has a smooth, broad, symmetric axial high, rather than the deep, wide, asymmetric central rift valley typically seen in slow-spreading mid-ocean ridges.

The northern EPR, or the boundary between the Pacific and Cocos plates, is considered a fast-spreading ridge, and it has had a full rate of spreading of around ~110 mm/yr for the past 2 million years.
The southern EPR, or the boundary between the Pacific and Nazca plates, is considered a superfast spreading ridge, meaning that it spreads with a full rate of >130-150 mm/yr.
The fastest rates of spreading are between the Easter Microplate and the Garrett Transform, where there is a full spreading rate between 150-155 mm/yr.
There two stable triple junctions across the EPR, which are the Galápagos triple junction and the Chile triple junction.

The Galápagos triple junction is a ridge-ridge-ridge junction where the Pacific, Nazca, and Cocos plates meet, while the Chile triple junction is a ridge-trench-trench junction where the South American, Nazca, and Antarctic plates meet.
